Lakeside Logistics — Paid Sick Leave Policy (Section 4.2)
Paid sick leave accrues based on tenure at Lakeside Logistics:
- Under 1 year of tenure: no company-paid sick leave beyond the state-mandated minimum (3 days/year).
- 1 year up to 3 years of tenure: 5 paid sick days per year.

state:
NimbusTech HR Policy — Parental Leave (v3)
1. Primary caregivers receive 12 weeks of parental leave at 100% pay.
2. Secondary caregivers receive 4 weeks of parental leave at 100% pay.
3. Eligibility requires at least 6 months of continuous employment as of the leave start date.
4. Leave must begin within 60 days of the birth or placement of the child. If leave is not started within that window, it is forfeited.
5. Exception: if the child requires a NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) stay, the 60-day window instead runs from the date of the infant's discharge from the NICU, not from the date of birth.
6. Parental leave dates must be requested in writing to HR at least 2 weeks before the intended start date, except when the delay is itself caused by a NICU stay, in which case shorter notice is accepted.
7. Parental leave may be taken intermittently (in separate blocks) only with advance written approval from both the employee's manager and HR; otherwise it must be taken in one continuous block.
8. Parental leave runs concurrently with any leave taken under state family leave law, where applicable, and does not extend the total protected leave period beyond what state law provides.

Coastal Retail Group — Overtime Compensation Election
Non-exempt employees who work overtime may elect, at the time overtime is requested, either (a) cash payout at 1.5x their regular rate, or (b) compensatory ('comp') time off at 1.5 hours of comp time per overtime hour worked. If no election is made, the default is cash payout. Comp time must be used within 90 days of being earned; any comp time not used within that window is automatically paid out in cash at the 1.5x rate.

Case: employee Wes Okoro earned 6 hours of comp time exactly 100 days ago, having explicitly elected comp time at the time. He has not used any of it.

questions.instruction: What should happen to Wes's unused comp time now?

candidates.description: It remains available for him to use going forward
It is forfeited entirely
It is automatically paid out in cash at 1.5x
It is converted into regular PTO

questions.notes: 100 days exceeds the 90-day use-it window, triggering automatic cash payout.

questions.instruction: Can Wes still choose to use this comp time for a future day off?
questions.notes: Past the 90-day window it converts automatically to cash; it's no longer usable as time off.

questions.instruction: Which of the following are true about Wes's comp time election?

candidates.description: He explicitly elected comp time rather than cash payout
He is still within the 90-day window to use it
His election defaulted to cash payout because he made no choice
He forfeits the comp time entirely with no payout at all

questions.notes: He made an explicit election and is past 90 days, but that triggers cash payout, not forfeiture.

state:
Coastal Retail Group — Fair Pay Policy, Overtime Eligibility
Only employees formally classified as non-exempt are eligible for overtime pay (1.5x regular rate beyond 40 hours/week). Employees classified as exempt (salaried roles meeting the executive, administrative, or professional duties tests under wage-and-hour law) are not eligible for overtime pay regardless of hours worked, while they remain classified as exempt. An employee who believes their actual day-to-day duties do not match their exempt classification may request a duties-test review from HR. If HR determines the role should be reclassified as non-exempt, the reclassification applies prospectively from the date HR completes the review, not retroactively - unless HR's review finds the original classification was made in error, in which case back pay may be considered.

Email thread:

From: Renee Castillo (Assistant Store Manager)
To: HR-Payroll
Date: Oct 2
Subject: Overtime for last week

Hi HR,

I'm salaried as an Assistant Manager, but honestly my day-to-day is almost identical to our hourly cashiers - I ring up customers, restock shelves, and run the register during rushes. I rarely supervise anyone directly since we're short-staffed; that's usually the Store Manager's job. I've been in this role for about 14 months now, if that's relevant. I worked 50 hours last week covering shifts. Can I get overtime for the extra 10 hours?

Thanks,
Renee

From: HR-Payroll
To: Renee Castillo
Date: Oct 3
Subject: RE: Overtime for last week

Hi Renee,

I hear you, and I want to look into this properly. As things stand, you're currently classified as exempt, so unfortunately the 50 hours last week aren't eligible for overtime pay under that classification - that's true regardless of how many hours are worked while exempt.

That said, what you're describing sounds worth reviewing. I'm going to open a duties-test review to see whether your day-to-day work matches an exempt role or not. If we determine the classification should change, that would apply going forward - and if we find the original classification was simply wrong from the start, we'd also look at back pay for the affected period. I'll follow up once the review is done; it usually takes about two weeks. In the meantime, your classification and pay stay unchanged, and it may help to keep a short log of your typical daily tasks in case it's useful for the review.

Best,
HR Payroll

From: Renee Castillo
To: HR-Payroll
Date: Oct 3
Subject: RE: RE: Overtime for last week

Understood, thanks for looking into it. Let me know what you find.

questions.instruction: Does Renee's current (exempt) classification entitle her to overtime pay for the 50 hours she worked?
questions.notes: While classified exempt, no overtime applies regardless of actual hours or duties.

questions.instruction: What is HR doing in response to Renee's email?

candidates.description: Paying overtime immediately for the 50 hours
Denying the request with no further action
Opening a duties-test review of her actual role
Automatically reclassifying her as non-exempt effective immediately

questions.notes: HR opens a review rather than paying, denying outright, or reclassifying immediately.

questions.instruction: Which of the following are true based on the email thread?

candidates.description: Renee is not entitled to overtime pay under her current classification
A duties-test review could change her classification going forward
Renee is guaranteed back pay for the 50 hours no matter what the review finds
Renee's own description of her duties immediately reclassified her as non-exempt

questions.notes: Back pay is only possible under a specific finding, not guaranteed; her description alone changes nothing by itself.

questions.instruction: If HR's review finds the original exempt classification was made in error, could Renee receive back pay for the affected period?
questions.notes: Policy explicitly allows back pay consideration only in that specific error scenario.

state: Coastal Retail Group holiday pay policy: employees who work on a company-recognized holiday receive 2x their regular pay for hours worked that day. Holiday-premium hours do not count toward the 40-hour weekly threshold used to calculate overtime; regular (non-holiday) hours worked that same week are evaluated separately for overtime. Employee Ines Okonjo worked 8 hours on Thanksgiving (a recognized holiday) and 36 regular hours the rest of that week - 44 total hours worked.

questions.instruction: Is Ines owed 1.5x overtime pay in addition to her 2x holiday pay this week?
questions.notes: Holiday hours are excluded from the OT threshold; her 36 regular hours don't exceed 40.

questions.instruction: How is Ines's pay calculated for her Thanksgiving hours?

candidates.description: 1x her regular rate
1.5x her regular rate
2x her regular rate, with no added overtime
2x her regular rate plus an additional 1.5x overtime premium

questions.notes: She gets the 2x holiday rate; no overtime is triggered since non-holiday hours (36) stay under 40.

state:
Meridian Financial Group — Overtime Approval Policy
Overtime must be pre-approved by the employee's supervisor at least 24 hours before the overtime is worked. Exception: during the year-end blackout period (December 15-31), all overtime requires Director-level approval regardless of how much advance notice is given, due to year-end budget close procedures; supervisor approval alone is not sufficient during this window, even for routine, pre-planned overtime.

Case: Farrukh Tashkentov's team had been under a tight deadline all month to close out several client accounts before year-end reporting. On December 20, his supervisor verbally approved 5 hours of overtime that same day, for a rush year-end order.

questions.instruction: Was this overtime properly approved per policy?
questions.notes: December 20 falls in the year-end blackout window, which needs Director-level approval, not just a supervisor's.

questions.instruction: What approval was actually required for this overtime request?

candidates.description: No approval was required
Supervisor approval with at least 24 hours' notice
Supervisor approval given the same day is sufficient
Director-level approval, regardless of notice given

questions.notes: Dec 15-31 blackout requires Director-level approval regardless of notice.

questions.instruction: Which of the following approval requirements did Farrukh's overtime satisfy?

candidates.description: At least 24 hours' advance notice was given
A supervisor approved the request
A Director approved the request
The request fell outside the year-end blackout period

questions.notes: Only supervisor approval was obtained, which is insufficient inside the blackout window.
